quotes.text: Perhaps we might be expected to admire «The Originator» simply for sticking to his guns at an age when rock'n'roll was temporarily going out of style and the wild men of the Fifties were expected to «mature», soften up, and re-orient their output at audiences that craved craft and gloss over aggressive energy.
Bo Diddley's blessing-and-curse is a lot like Lemmy's: he is just what he is, and changing too much is impossible for him on a physiological level.

'Aztec' takes the Latin-influenced side of such Bo Diddley's songs as 'Crackin' Up' and expands it to a full-fledged foray into Mexican territory (cue the name), with an experimental solo that is mostly composed of disjointed, choppy, twangy, sliding licks creating a proto-psychedelic feel.

Given that 'Aztec' is unquestionably the album's most creative composition, settling this question some day would be important, but since both involved parties are already dead, we'll have to wait until we join them both in Heaven to conduct a proper confrontation.

We can only guess how all those albums might have sounded like if the Bo Diddley / Peggy Jones partnership was more of an actual partnership and less of a «look-at-me-I'm-so-cool, I-have-a-chick-playing-guitar-in-my-band» sort of situation.

The instrumentals are arguably the most interesting songs on the album: in addition to 'Aztec', there is also 'Congo', which threatens to be just an instrumental recreation of 'Roadrunner' in the opening bars but then quickly turns into a piece of exciting twangy rockabilly that probably does not have much to do with 'Congo' but has everything to do with, let's say, Bo Diddley playing Chuck Berry with a typically Bo Diddley sound.

The song is rhythmically similar to hambone, a technique of dancing and slapping various parts of the body to create a rhythm and song. Diddley's electric guitar along with his backup musicians on maracas and drums contributed to the patted juba rhythm. This fusion of rock and roll, African rhythms, and guitar was a breakthrough and became known as the Bo Diddley Beat.

Music critic Richie Unterberger described the song as: soaked with futuristic waves of tremolo guitar, set to an ageless nursery rhyme ... The result was not exactly blues, or even straight R&B, but a new kind of guitar-based rock 'n' roll, soaked in the blues and R&B, but owing allegiance to neither.
quotes.publication: All Music Guide to the Blues

quotes.text: Bo Diddley was a real pioneer, one of the great sore thumbs in the traditional rock roll call: Bill Haley, Elvis Presley, Chuck Berry, Jerry Lee Lewis, Little Richard and (if you're cool) Gene Vincent. Then there's Bo Diddley with his "Bo Diddley beat," songs unapologetically about himself and backwoods folklore – a far cry from the hot rods and young love that were the staples of 50s rock and roll.

The album gets started with Gun Slinger, a myth-making song spinning a ridiculous yarn "about Bo Diddley at the O.K. Corral." One way or another, all the other songs on the record tie into this rough-hewn and spirited little invention but what really fascinates about it is its musical emptiness.
It's got a believable rapport coming from Bo's add-libbing talents ("you been eatin' regular, huh?").
Surreally, the first line of "Somewhere Over the Rainbow" is kiped for Somewhere, a slow ballad sung in a touchingly sincere and roughshod manner.

An energetic (hardest rocker in the set!) cover of a Tennessee Ernie Ford hit. The lyric actually utilizes history, in the form of coal mining and debt bondage, rather than rely on western fantasyland tropes, which helps me take it seriously. Tennessee Ernie Ford's version was an infectious slice of finger-popping cheese – Bo put the blood back in it and that makes his the definitive version to me.
Bo could sing this stuff and make you believe in it.
its 12 songs are exemplary of the Bo Diddley beat: "This is one of the greatest rock sounds that you're likely to hear, and it's all on this one record, too."
